profiles.title: The Stone Sky
profiles.author: N. K. Jemisin
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: Orbit published the third Broken Earth novel in 2017; the 2018 Hugo is an award date, not publication date.

profiles.genre_and_form: Speculative post-apocalyptic literary fantasy; trilogy conclusion

series.name: The Broken Earth
series.sequence_status: Third and last novel: substantial prior-book revelations are assumed. Read after The Fifth Season and The Obelisk Gate for narrative comprehension; your queue can still be manually reordered.

profiles.summary: The final Broken Earth book returns to a world that has learned to survive recurring ecological catastrophe through coercion and violent exclusion. Its central parent-child relationship turns the survival question into a moral one: what should people preserve when their institutions have repeatedly taught them to hurt others? This profile intentionally omits the outcomes of the first two books and the trilogy’s ending.
profiles.author_and_work_background: N. K. Jemisin’s third Broken Earth volume followed The Fifth Season and The Obelisk Gate. The Stone Sky won the 2018 Hugo for Best Novel, part of the trilogy’s unusual sequence of three consecutive Best Novel wins. Publication chronology should not be confused with the timing of events inside this multi-voiced narrative.
profiles.before_reading: Treat this as a closing argument, not an entry point. Before opening it, jot down your questions from books one and two without asking the app to summarize their answers. Track decisions about cooperation, punishment, and historical truth as they arise; reserve final evaluation until you actually finish.
profiles.literary_approach: The series shifts perspective, time, and distance between storyteller and characters; second-person narration is a deliberate device rather than a conventional omniscient summary. The ending invites readers to reassess how a world’s institutions explain themselves. This is a literary interpretation, not proof that the text settles every political question.
profiles.context: Orbit’s synopsis confirms third-in-trilogy placement and the stakes of a damaged world; Hugo records confirm the award. Claims about voice, embodied power and responsibility below are editorial reading prompts, not quotations or an assertion that every character arc has been independently audited.

themes.label: Repair versus retribution
themes.discussion: When a society survives through organized harm, what could repair actually require?

themes.label: Who narrates catastrophe
themes.discussion: Notice whose perspective becomes intelligible and whose experience is reduced to a category.

themes.label: Intergenerational choice
themes.discussion: How does responsibility change when children inherit an exhausted world?

profiles.personal_fit: For the user’s interest in morally complex fantasy and close, emotionally grounded prose, this offers an unusually intense final thematic discussion.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The series’ inventiveness, second-person voice and traumatic material demand attention; do not treat it as an easy standalone break between nonfiction titles.

notes: Apocalyptic disaster, death and collective violence
Coercion, social exclusion and trauma involving families; not an exhaustive scene list

profiles.title: Notes from Underground
profiles.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: Originally published in 1864 in Russian; listed translations are later editorial products.

profiles.genre_and_form: Russian philosophical novella; first-person polemic and confessional fiction

series.name: Standalone Russian novella
series.sequence_status: No numbered sequel; belongs to Dostoevsky’s wider intellectual development.

profiles.summary: A bitter, self-consciously intelligent man speaks directly to the reader, disputing tidy predictions of human happiness and exposing his own appetites for humiliation and control. The second part turns the abstractions into remembered encounters where he cannot act as the lucid moral agent he claims to be. Listening to the contradictions is more revealing than deciding whether he is simply correct or incorrect.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Dostoevsky published Notes from Underground in 1864, between the earlier experiences of exile and his major later novels. The Penguin and Vintage publisher listings identify Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky as translators of named modern editions; this does NOT settle which English diction should be chosen for the reader or prove a particular owned ISBN. The narrator is not automatically a reliable spokesman for Dostoevsky.
profiles.before_reading: Read the opening as a performance by a hostile, self-interrupting mind. Keep separate columns for what the speaker says people want, what he actually does, and what you infer. Compare concepts rather than direct word-for-word quotations if you switch translators.
profiles.literary_approach: First-person address creates a trap: contempt and self-exposure arrive in the same sentence. The movement from abstract argument to embarrassing memory pressures any simple theory of rational self-interest; repeated qualifications and spite are central to the voice.
profiles.context: The narrative responds to nineteenth-century intellectual confidence in rational social design. Oxford’s discussion of St Petersburg helps situate its deliberately abstract geography, while the publisher’s translator credits confirm only edition particulars. The broader relationship to rational egoism is interpretive historical context, not an edition certification.

themes.label: The will against calculation
themes.discussion: Can a person choose something harmful to resist being reduced to a formula?

themes.label: Self-knowledge without change
themes.discussion: Why can precise self-description coexist with repeated cruelty?

themes.label: Untrustworthy confession
themes.discussion: What does a confession try to gain from the audience?

profiles.personal_fit: An excellent compact companion to the philosophy commitments: argumentative, abrasive, and unusually valuable for probing contradictions in moral psychology.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The narrator is intentionally unpleasant; interpreting him as an author-endorsed lesson will flatten the book.

notes: Psychological distress and self-loathing
Cruelty, humiliation, misogyny and emotionally harmful interactions; non-exhaustive

discussion_questions: Does freedom require the capacity to choose against one’s welfare?

profiles.title: The Color of Law
profiles.author: Richard Rothstein
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: First published by Liveright in 2017; edition and pagination vary.

profiles.genre_and_form: US housing policy history; argumentative nonfiction

series.name: Standalone nonfiction
series.sequence_status: Not part of a numbered series.

profiles.summary: Rothstein contests the comforting idea that racially divided American neighborhoods were chiefly the unintended sum of personal preference and private prejudice. He assembles examples of federal, state and local decision-making to argue that government helped construct and maintain the segregation visible today. The book asks whether identifying constitutional state action changes what the public owes in remedy.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Color of Law appeared with Liveright in 2017. Rothstein’s Economic Policy Institute material and an American Bar Association interview articulate his de jure segregation thesis; a later EPI piece is explicitly his response to a critique, not an independent confirmation that critics were refuted. Independent reviews and historical scholarship should accompany this account.
profiles.before_reading: Keep a three-column evidence log: policy or law, documented effect, and the inference the author draws. Note distinctions between discriminatory public rules and private conduct. When you read competing analyses, identify whether they disagree about facts, scale of causation or choice of remedy.
profiles.literary_approach: Case studies turn legal categories into concrete neighborhood histories. The argument relies on accumulating policy examples and showing how they worked together; examples deserve separate checking rather than treating the word systemic as self-evident proof.
profiles.context: The book intervenes in disputes over government responsibility for residential segregation and what remedies follow from that history. EPI hosts the author’s position and rebuttal; the ABA interview clarifies that argument; an independent Publishers Weekly review confirms its reception, not every historical inference.

themes.label: Government versus market stories
themes.discussion: How does responsibility change when a pattern is treated as the result of policy?

themes.label: Evidence and moral obligation
themes.discussion: What kind of historical finding justifies a present-day remedy?

themes.discussion: Do de jure/de facto labels illuminate causation or oversimplify interacting forces?

profiles.personal_fit: An evidence-heavy counterpart to your required ethics and political philosophy, offering specific claims worth testing.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The narrative is an argument with contested causal emphases, not a neutral exhaustive history of every metropolitan area.

profiles.title: The Colour of Magic
profiles.author: Terry Pratchett
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: Official Pratchett estate dates original publication to 24 November 1983.

profiles.genre_and_form: Comic high fantasy; episodic fantasy parody

series.name: Discworld — Wizards
series.sequence_status: Wizards opener and first published Discworld novel; your manual queue does not enforce sequential order.

profiles.summary: An anxious wizard, Rincewind, unexpectedly becomes an interpreter of the Discworld for a relentlessly curious visitor, Twoflower. Their travelogue sweeps across exaggerated fantasy settings while the narrator keeps dismantling supposedly heroic behavior. It is an invitation to enjoy invention, not a reliable map of how every later Discworld novel will feel.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The Colour of Magic was published in 1983 and launched Pratchett’s Discworld. The estate and current publisher place it first among the Wizards novels. The early work targets familiar sword-and-sorcery tropes; later Discworld books develop different social and institutional forms of satire, so this should not be treated as a representative sample of the entire mature series.
profiles.before_reading: Approach the book as connected episodes rather than a tightly unified quest with a single arc. Catch the contrast between the earnest tourist’s perspective and Rincewind’s survival instincts. You can choose another Discworld book next; if you choose The Light Fantastic, know it continues these events.
profiles.literary_approach: Rapid changes of scene and genre pastiche let Pratchett destabilize the fantasy hero, magical peril and exotic traveler. Joke density sometimes substitutes for character interiority: a deliberate stylistic tradeoff, not a sign that the series lacks later depth.
profiles.context: The publication chronology and estate’s 40-year retrospective establish a 1983 series origin. The modern official reading guidance acknowledges flexible entry points; for these first two books, however, narrative continuity is stronger than with many later independent Discworld arcs.

profiles.title: Utilitarianism
profiles.author: John Stuart Mill
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: First appeared as three magazine installments in 1861; standalone book publication followed in 1863 and a corrected second edition in 1864.

profiles.genre_and_form: Moral philosophy essay and public argument
profiles.summary: Mill defends the ethical importance of happiness while attempting to rescue utilitarian reasoning from the charge that it counts only crude sensation or encourages selfish calculation. He distinguishes qualities of pleasure, explains moral motivation and social sanctions, and offers a much-disputed attempt to establish why happiness should be pursued as an end.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The essay appeared in Fraser’s Magazine in 1861 and book form in 1863; Cambridge identifies its later corrected 1864 second edition. The public-domain historical text and today’s edited scholarly editions are related but not identical bibliographic objects. Mill’s argument should also be read alongside his views of liberty and social reform, without assuming the book contains all of those positions.
profiles.before_reading: Build a tiny glossary for happiness, utility, pleasure, higher/lower, justice, proof and sanction. After each section rewrite Mill’s strongest claim as one testable proposition. Compare his reasoning with Kant or Aristotle rather than deciding which philosopher wins by rhetorical confidence alone.
profiles.literary_approach: Mill anticipates hostile objections, draws distinctions and moves from practical common moral judgments toward theoretical justification. The most contested passage is not merely a slogan about greatest happiness but his proposed proof and its interpretation.
profiles.context: Stanford’s philosophical essays discuss both the continuing relevance and objections to Mill’s qualitative pleasures, internal sanctions and apparent inference from what people desire to what is desirable. Cambridge’s historical notes establish the magazine/book distinction.

themes.label: Kinds of happiness
themes.discussion: Are some pleasures meaningfully better without relying on social snobbery?

themes.discussion: Can social feeling support obligation, or is it only useful pressure?

themes.discussion: What would count as evidence for a moral end?

profiles.personal_fit: A central readable text for your 2027 ethics commitment and a useful contrast with Kant, Aristotle and everyday moral dilemmas.
profiles.possible_mismatch: Its accessible rhetoric can conceal rapid argumentative leaps; a companion commentary helps but should not replace Mill’s primary text.

profiles.title: A Wizard of Earthsea
profiles.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: First published by Parnassus Press in 1968, per the author’s bibliography and estate.

series.name: Earthsea
series.sequence_status: Earthsea beginning; first of the original trilogy, followed by The Tombs of Atuan and The Farthest Shore.

profiles.summary: Young Ged has a remarkable gift and the dangerous belief that skill can secure his identity. His education as a wizard begins amid naming, discipline and an error that forces him to reckon with consequences he would rather escape. Earthsea’s archipelago is precise and spare, with magic bound to language and responsibility instead of unrestricted wish-fulfillment.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Le Guin’s first Earthsea novel appeared in 1968 with Parnassus Press. Her own essays explain that the people of the Archipelago, including Ged, were not imagined as default white heroes, and that visual adaptations and packaging have sometimes obscured this. The National Endowment for the Arts features the novel in its Big Read materials.
profiles.before_reading: Track names carefully: who gets to name something, what such knowledge permits, and when withholding a name protects someone. Note the difference between skill and judgment in Ged’s teachers. Resist the temptation to import later Earthsea revelations into the first novel.
profiles.literary_approach: Le Guin compresses years of development into lucid, almost folktale-like prose. Repetition, balance, island geography and restrained dialogue make ethical questions feel inseparable from the enchantment; interpretive weight often falls on what is not said.
profiles.context: Le Guin’s essays about fantasy representation challenge the assumption that heroes of epic fantasy are naturally European or white; her intended character descriptions are author statements, not outside guesses. Earthsea’s larger sequence also evolved beyond what the first book initially anticipated.

profiles.possible_mismatch: Readers expecting relentless combat or sprawling exposition may initially find its fable-like distance quiet.

profiles.title: Crime and Punishment
profiles.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: Published in The Russian Messenger in monthly installments in 1866; modern book editions and English translations differ.

profiles.genre_and_form: Russian psychological and philosophical crime novel
profiles.summary: An impoverished former student in Saint Petersburg persuades himself that an exceptional person might be entitled to step outside ordinary moral rules. A violent crime sets his theory against his bodily fear, confused motives and ties to other people. The novel’s suspense asks less whether he can state his premise than whether human consciousness can remain obedient to it.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Crime and Punishment appeared across 1866 installments of The Russian Messenger. University of Toronto’s exhibition highlights its translation history. English readers can encounter Oliver Ready (Penguin), Nicolas Pasternak Slater with Sarah J. Young’s editorial material (Oxford), or Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky (Vintage/PRH). Those editions have different phrasing and apparatus. None is independently confirmed as the reader’s chosen copy.
profiles.before_reading: Keep a modest cast list and note the recurring gap between Raskolnikov’s theoretical justifications and what his body or relationships reveal. If comparing translations, check the same scene across editions rather than quoting page numbers as though they were universal. Avoid adaptations until you have formed your own reading.
profiles.literary_approach: Suffocating rooms, the city’s oppressive movement, feverish dialogue and close access to unstable thinking produce a pressure-cooker rhythm. The narrative repeatedly shifts between intellectual abstraction and the stubborn physical reality of consequences.
profiles.context: OUP’s work on St Petersburg emphasizes the planned city as both physical setting and figure for dangerous abstraction; the Toronto Library offers verifiable publication and translation context. Treat claims about Dostoevsky’s final moral message as critical interpretation rather than indisputable authorial intention.

profiles.title: How to Be an Antiracist
profiles.author: Ibram X. Kendi
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: One World published this book in 2019; edition formats vary.

profiles.genre_and_form: Political and social nonfiction; memoir-inflected conceptual argument

series.name: Standalone nonfiction
series.sequence_status: Not part of a numbered series.

profiles.summary: Kendi asks readers to distinguish passive self-description from actions and policies that sustain or reduce racial inequity. Personal episodes of mistakes and changed beliefs alternate with definitions and historical material; the book proposes an active rather than merely declarative standard of antiracist practice. It is an argument to evaluate, not a requirement to agree with every definition.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Released by One World in 2019, this book follows Kendi’s earlier historical writing with a more confessional, practical framework. Publishers Weekly and Kirkus document the blend of autobiography, terminology and policy claims. The New Yorker critically examines implications of the framework. A later Cambridge journal discussion shows scholarly debate has continued; it does not automatically validate every original proposal.
profiles.before_reading: For each introduced definition, write down the practical consequence and a possible difficult case. Separate Kendi’s account of his former beliefs from his present normative claims. Build a comparison grid with Rothstein’s housing-law history and McGhee’s account of shared public goods.
profiles.literary_approach: Definitions often open chapters, while self-critique turns the argument back on its speaker. Shifts between personal admission, conceptual taxonomy and public-policy recommendations invite readers to examine how the levels support one another.
profiles.context: Contemporary reviewers described both the clarity and uncompromising binary of racist/antiracist categories; critics dispute implications for culture, individual agency and policy evaluation. Present those as live disagreements, rather than claiming political consensus or imposing a required reaction.

themes.label: Labels versus behavior
themes.discussion: Does refusing a negative label demonstrate anything about outcomes?

themes.discussion: How would a reader establish whether a policy decreases inequity?

profiles.personal_fit: A useful discussion partner to your empirical nonfiction and normative ethics selections, especially if you actively scrutinize arguments.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The book’s firm categories and autobiographical voice can frustrate readers seeking a detached survey or quantified policy evaluation.

profiles.author: Terry Pratchett
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: Official estate records original publication on 2 June 1986.

profiles.genre_and_form: Comic fantasy and satire; direct continuation

series.name: Discworld — Wizards
series.sequence_status: Second Wizards installment and direct sequel to The Colour of Magic; user remains free to move it in queue.

profiles.summary: The chaos set in motion by The Colour of Magic continues with a reluctant wizard, an irrepressible tourist and a dangerous larger cosmic problem. Pratchett turns the apparently grand scale of magical catastrophe into a test of ordinary survival and absurd institutions. The premise is safe to know; plot solutions and the predecessor’s concluding beats are not described here.
profiles.author_and_work_background: The estate dates The Light Fantastic to 1986, three years after The Colour of Magic. Official reading guidance labels it the second Wizards book. Many Discworld stories offer independent starting points, but this is a closer continuation than most, so a reader who voluntarily shuffles it first will encounter unexplained prior events.
profiles.before_reading: Before reading, recall how Rincewind and Twoflower interpret danger differently, or start without recap if you prefer to discover the disorientation. Watch how sequel stakes enlarge and how Pratchett still punctures fantasy grandeur with everyday human reactions.
profiles.literary_approach: Expanding peril gives the sequel a clearer destination than the first book’s episodic tour, while interlocking gags and genre reversals keep the tone comic. The narrator often builds an epic expectation only to deflate it through physical inconvenience or social absurdity.
profiles.context: The author’s official publication record and Wizards listing establish a direct sequel. Official commentary about early Discworld as fantasy parody explains the different emphasis from later social novels; it is an interpretive guide, not a guarantee of every reader’s preference.

profiles.title: Existentialism Is a Humanism
profiles.author: Jean-Paul Sartre
profiles.verification_scope: Work-level bibliographic facts checked against title-specific listed sources on 2026-11-20. Interpretation is labelled editorial. This is not a complete text audit or verification of your privately owned translation, ISBN, audio duration, page count or every content warning.

publication.basis: Delivered orally 29 October 1945; commonly published in French in 1946; modern Yale translation is a separate 2007 edition.

series.name: Standalone philosophical lecture
series.sequence_status: Not part of a numbered narrative series.

profiles.summary: Sartre gives an unusually public-facing defense of existentialism against accusations of despair, moral irresponsibility and indifference to humanity. Without a ready-made human essence or a prior moral script, people must choose and answer for the lives they make, even as those choices carry meaning beyond one individual. The ease of stating the thesis should not disguise its difficult implications.
profiles.author_and_work_background: Sartre delivered the lecture at Club Maintenant on 29 October 1945, with publication following in 1946. The Yale University Press 2007 volume is Carol Macomber’s English translation and includes separate supplementary material; its contents should not be misattributed to the original oral event. Stanford’s scholarly treatment traces development and critical difficulties in Sartre’s ideas of freedom.
profiles.before_reading: Read the argument with two parallel questions: what does Sartre say a person can choose, and what constraints shape those choices? Compare the rhetoric of universal responsibility to actual social position. Mark the difference between an example intended to clarify and a proof establishing a principle.
profiles.literary_approach: The lecture’s directness, public objections and memorable formulations make it approachable but can compress substantial philosophical disputes. The movement from no predetermined essence to ethical responsibility is not a universally accepted deduction.
profiles.context: The public lecture answered critics in postwar France, while later existentialist debates explored embodied, economic and political situation. Stanford’s account highlights these tensions; Yale identifies an exact modern translated edition, not the reader’s owned copy.

themes.label: Freedom and situation
themes.discussion: What is chosen, and what is inherited?

themes.label: Responsibility as burden
themes.discussion: Why might freedom provoke anxiety rather than liberation?

themes.label: Humanism without predetermined essence
themes.discussion: What kind of shared ethics can arise without fixed human nature?

profiles.personal_fit: An accessible, provocative bridge between philosophical study and the Russian novels’ practical questions about choice.
profiles.possible_mismatch: The lecture simplifies positions and can overstate the power of choice; treating it as Sartre’s final philosophical system would mislead.

notes: Anxiety, abandonment, despair and morally difficult choices discussed philosophically
No edition-specific comprehensive content assessment
